pr_body:
* Pass nil to NewJSONLogger to avoid splitting stream
* Remove syncing stderr stream

Fixes https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/107033

#### What type of PR is
/kind bug

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

```release-note
Fix 1.23 performance regression in JSON logging caused by syncing stdout every time error was logged.
```

```docs

```
/cc @pohly
pr_comments: FYI @pohly I have noticed another strange thing. For log buffering we are using zapcore.BufferedWriteSyncer which maintains it's own flush loop that is independent from what Kubernetes has. Also it doesn't follow the design proposed by SIG Scalability in https://github.com/kubernetes/klog/issues/209 as it doesn't shred logs as proposed.

[APPROVALNOTIFIER] This PR is **APPROVED** This pull-request has been approved by: *pohly*, *serathius* The full list of commands accepted by this bot can be found [here](https://go.k8s.io/bot-commands?repo=kubernetes%2Fkubernetes). The pull request process is described [here](https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/guide/owners.md#the-code-review-process)
Needs approval from an approver in each of these files: - ~~[staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/logs/OWNERS](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/logs/OWNERS)~~ [pohly,serathius] Approvers can indicate their approval by writing `/approve` in a comment Approvers can cancel approval by writing `/approve cancel` in a comment

> For log buffering we are using zapcore.BufferedWriteSyncer which maintains it's own flush loop that is independent from what Kubernetes has.

I don't see that as a problem. The Kubernetes flushing at some point can be removed entirely in favor of letting the logging backend handle it - that's design proposed by Tim. Our current solution is not wrong, either: we do guarantee that logs get flushed at least as often as specified by `--log-flush-frequency`.

> Also it doesn't follow the design proposed by SIG Scalability in [kubernetes/klog#209](https://github.com/kubernetes/klog/issues/209) as it doesn't shred logs as proposed.

That was just "a draft idea" (i.e. not a requirement). What we have is a first alpha implementation of split streams that just reuses existing functionality. If something better is needed, we can iterate.

With "shred logs" you mean discarding unwritten log messages?

> > For log buffering we are using zapcore.BufferedWriteSyncer which maintains it's own flush loop that is independent from what Kubernetes has.
> 
> I don't see that as a problem. The Kubernetes flushing at some point can be removed entirely in favor of letting the logging backend handle it - that's design proposed by Tim. Our current solution is not wrong, either: we do guarantee that logs get flushed at least as often as specified by `--log-flush-frequency`.

Yes, that makes sense.

> > Also it doesn't follow the design proposed by SIG Scalability in [kubernetes/klog#209](https://github.com/kubernetes/klog/issues/209) as it doesn't shred logs as proposed.
> 
> That was just "a draft idea" (i.e. not a requirement). What we have is a first alpha implementation of split streams that just reuses existing functionality. If something better is needed, we can iterate.

Would be good to get some feedback from SIG Scalability, I'm not sure if they had chance to take a look.

> With "shred logs" you mean discarding unwritten log messages?

Yes, I borrowed the term from server dropping lower priority requests when it detects it's overloaded.

issue_context.title: Regression in JSON logging throughput
issue_context.body:
### What happened?

When working on https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/107029 I have found a regression in JSON logging format that happend in 1.23.

In v1.23 JSON logging introduced two new features, log stream splitting and info log buffering. When I started measuring throughput it looked very promising, for example for info logs showed 10x improvement when using JSON split stream and 100Mi info log buffer. However when I introduced mixed logs (ever X info logs write 1 error logs), I noticed a large regression. For 10% of error logs written (apiserver during upgrade can write even 30% errors), I have found that just switching json on, results in log throughput being reduced from 25 MiB/s to 0.7MiB. 

I have bisected git repo and found that https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/commit/b22263d8351e873961aeff5d065faf3443de9acb was the root cause.
I expect that this regression would be noticed if we run scalability tests with JSON enabled.

Loader code: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/107032

/wg structured-logging
/cc @pohly
/sig scalability

### What did you expect to happen?

JSON should generate similar or greater log throughput when compared to text format.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run loader as described in README.md from https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/107032

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

### Kubernetes version

N/A

N/A

N/A

So to reproduce the regression, I need to do `go run ./staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/logs/loader/cmd/logger.go --logging-format=json 1>/tmp/stdout.out 2>/tmp/stderr.out` (default for error rate is 10%, 300 for message length, 10s duration) for old and new code, right?

Yes, let me give my results.

Before text: 30.7MiB/s, json:39.6MiB/s
```
kubernetes $ go run ./staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/logs/loader/cmd/logger.go --logging-format=text  1>/tmp/stdout.out 2> /tmp/stderr.out && du  /tmp/*.out
315072  /tmp/stderr.out
0       /tmp/stdout.out
kubernetes $ go run ./staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/logs/loader/cmd/logger.go --logging-format=json 1>/tmp/stdout.out 2> /tmp/stderr.out && du  /tmp/*.out
0       /tmp/stderr.out
405592  /tmp/stdout.out
```

After, text: 30.6MiB/s, json: 6.5MiB/s
```
kubernetes $ go run ./staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/logs/loader/cmd/logger.go --logging-format=text 1>/tmp/stdout.out 2> /tmp/stderr.out && du  /tmp/*.out
313672  /tmp/stderr.out
0       /tmp/stdout.out
kubernetes $ go run ./staging/src/k8s.io/component-base/logs/loader/cmd/logger.go --logging-format=json 1>/tmp/stdout.out 2> /tmp/stderr.out && du  /tmp/*.out
0       /tmp/stderr.out
67124   /tmp/stdout.out
```

> After discussion on the #release-management Slack channel [1], we decided to cut Kubernetes 1.23.1 patch release on Thursday, December 16.

should we try to get this in 1.23.1?

@aojea Yes, we just moved JSON and Structured Logging to Beta in v1.23. This bug should cause performance issues when there is non trivial amount of errors (>1%) written by control plane. I expect that this has really bad impact on upgrades which I have seen can reach 30% of error logs from apiserver.

It's worth pointing out that this regression only occurs when writing to a disk-based file (see https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/107032#issuecomment-995933422).

That also provides a very likely explanation for the huge performance difference: I bet zap not only flushes its buffered info messages, it also syncs the file. That is fast for tmpfs, but slow for real disks.

review_comments:
This part is clearly a bug. It's the result of a last-minute API change of `NewJSONLogger` from "pass two identical streams to avoid split streams" to "pass nil as second stream".

So passing nil here achieves the stated goal of this commit and PR. However, explaining that in the commit message and PR description would be useful.
Removing this is a loss of functionality that isn't described explicitly. Are you sure that this is better? If you remove the code, the comment also would need to be updated.

I'm looking into implementing buffer flushing instead of syncing whole pipeline, however I don't think this would achieve proper ordering as described in comment. I don't think that keeping logs ordered was ever goal, it's good property for human readable logs. It's good that we maintain this property by default, however when splitting stream is enabled I don't see a reason to sacrifice throughput as most log processing solutions don't care about order. It's even expected that logs are processed out of order, for example I have seen this behavior in Fluentbit.

I was thinking of the case where stdout and stderr get redirected into the same file or pipe and then get processed. But you are probably right, what matters in the end is just the time stamp attached to each message, not the order. So dropping the syncing between the two streams can indeed be dropped if we can't make it faster.

That it is this slow is a bit surprising. I'd like to understand better where the slowdown really comes from (mutex contention? slow Sync()).

Another thought: when both streams go to the same file descriptor, can we guarantee that log messages are written atomically?

Otherwise we could end up with interleaved log messages (`<start of message 1><message 2><end of message 1>`).
`writeWithFlushing` didn't handle that because no lock is held while writing.

> Another thought: when both streams go to the same file descriptor, can we guarantee that log messages are written atomically?

I don't think so. It's up to log consumer to merge streams, if it not able to keep up with producer generating to much data to one of the streams it is expected to interleave streams to avoid starving the other one. This is what I expect to happen from bash pipe merging, there will be no interleaving as long as volume of logs is reasonable, however it cannot guarantee this in high load scenarios. 

The only way to handle it would be to have application log aware merger that will be able to recognize when single log message starts and end. We technically could implement such functionality in kube-log-runner, however I don't think it's worth it. As splitting streams is an optional feature, it's much more reasonable to document this behavior so users are aware of this behavior when enabling this feature.

So we document that split stream assumes independent streams. Works for me.

I'm wondering whether we then want another mode: single stream with buffering of info messages. That might provide some performance benefit (to be measured) at the risk of loosing in-memory messages in case of a crash.
